source.title: Exploring Memorization in Adversarial Training
source.authors: Yin-Peng Dong; Ke Xu; Xiao Yang; Tianyu Pang; Zhijie Deng; Hang Su; Jun Zhu

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text includes the paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization and train/test behavior under adversarial training, an extension of the standard-training setting in V1.
record.gate_note: The paper tests adversarial training, not the standard-training recipes named in the claim. Its random-label results and robust generalization measures concern adversarial examples and robust accuracy; these do not test V2–V8 as specified. Cited findings from other studies are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study tests V1 in adversarial training: Table A.1 reports natural train/test accuracy for the same architecture and recipe on true and random labels. Its dropout comparisons also test V6 in this setting. Robust accuracy and robust sharpness analyses alone do not test the corresponding natural-generalization claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly summarizes the convergence and complexity-measure conclusions but omits the principal robust-overfitting conclusion. The authors argue that excessive memorization of one-hot labels causes robust overfitting and report that temporal ensembling substantially mitigates it. They also identify weight-loss-landscape flatness as more reliable than the other tested complexity measures.
record.recipe_differences: Adversarial training with PGD-AT or TRADES; the claim versions primarily specify standard training or other interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, architecture, threat model and perturbation budget affect whether adversarial training converges; optimizer and learning-rate schedule changes did not make PGD-AT converge with random labels in the tested configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: True-label TRADES has a 62.18-point robust generalization gap without explicit regularization; random-label robust training accuracy varies substantially across regularizer configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial memorization and robust generalization depend on the training recipe and regularizers.

fits_no_version.finding: Several tested complexity measures fail to order robust generalization gaps; weight-loss-landscape flatness is comparatively more reliable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Complexity measures developed or used for adversarial training do not uniformly explain robust generalization.

record.problems: The main claim-version overlap is limited because the experiments use adversarial training. Some findings are presented in figures without numerical values in the text; uncertainty is not reported for the memorization results.
record.rows_left_out: No cited prior-work results were extracted. Figure-only complexity-measure comparisons in Fig. 6 and other figure-only learning curves were left out because the text does not give their numerical values.

untested.parts: The original standard-training architectures and recipes; ImageNet.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of learned local connections.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on held-out performance; optimizer experiments here concern convergence.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Very small training sets, excessive dropout, fully connected classifiers, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness ranking natural generalization gaps against norm and margin measures. The study instead analyzes robust gaps with different complexity measures.
Removal of examples selected by label-memorization influence versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: Natural true-label training/test accuracies for unregularized TRADES: 99.73% and 77.53%. These complete the coexistence comparison with R2.
missing.locator: Table A.1, first true-label row; Appendix A.3

missing.what: Natural train/test results for the other five regularizer configurations on both true and random labels. True-label test accuracy ranges from 77.31% to 84.26%; random-label training accuracy remains 99.15%–99.84% and test accuracy 9.04%–10.13%.

Controlled dropout comparisons on true labels: without augmentation or weight decay, natural test accuracy rises 77.53% to 79.96%; with weight decay and no augmentation, it rises 77.31% to 80.28%. Dropout rate is 0.2.
The stated perturbation-budget boundary for random-label PGD-AT convergence: it converges at 1/255 but fails at budgets of at least 2/255 in the tested configurations.

record.verdict_notes: Adversarial training is a new recipe, but its natural train/test measurements directly bear on V1 and V6. Untested original settings are not evidence against either version. No uncertainty is reported for Table A.1, although separate mitigation experiments report three-run mean/std results in Table C.2.

versions.untested_parts: Standard training; the named Inception, AlexNet and MLP settings; held-out accuracy on natural examples for true-label training.

rows.subject: WRN-28-10
rows.operation_detail: PGD-AT adversarial training on true or random labels
rows.value: With true labels both methods reach almost 100% natural and robust training accuracy; with random labels PGD-AT fails to converge while TRADES reaches nearly 100% training accuracies.
rows.note: The reported result concerns adversarial training accuracy; it does not supply held-out accuracy for this comparison.
rows.check: Split this aggregate into PGD-AT and TRADES, true and random labels, and natural and robust measures. The operation names PGD-AT but the value includes TRADES. Natural training results bear on V1's fitting component; robust training results do not independently establish natural generalization. Random-label convergence differs between the two algorithms.

source_check.correct: Split by algorithm, labeling and measure. Both algorithms achieve almost 100% natural and robust training accuracy on true labels. On random labels, PGD-AT fails to converge; TRADES reaches nearly 100% training accuracy. For PGD-AT, almost-perfect random-label fitting is absent. Training accuracies alone cannot determine V1's full coexistence effect.
source_check.problem: The PGD-AT operation includes TRADES results; partial conflates different algorithms and does not establish V1's held-out component.
